lesson.title: Building Tuples: Commas Do the Work
lesson.summary: Tuples are created with comma-separated values, not with parentheses, which explains both why a single-item tuple needs a trailing comma and how the tuple() constructor builds one from any iterable.
lesson.body:
You already know a Tuple as an ordered, immutable sequence, usually written with parentheses like (3, 4). What is easy to miss is that the parentheses are not what actually creates the tuple. The comma is. Parentheses are just grouping punctuation, the same symbols you would use to control order of operations in math; Python only treats a parenthesized group as a tuple because there happen to be commas inside it.

point = (3, 4)
colors = "red", "green", "blue"
single_item = (5,)
not_a_tuple = (5)

print(type(colors), colors)
print(type(single_item), single_item)
print(type(not_a_tuple), not_a_tuple)

The first print shows <class 'tuple'> ('red', 'green', 'blue'), proving that colors became a tuple even though it was never written with parentheses at all. The second shows <class 'tuple'> (5,): the trailing comma is what makes single_item a genuine one-element tuple. The third print is the trap this lesson exists to prevent: (5) has no comma, so Python just sees the number 5 wrapped in parentheses, and not_a_tuple turns out to be <class 'int'> 5, a plain integer, not a tuple at all.

Besides writing values out directly, you can build a tuple from any existing iterable using the tuple() constructor, which is especially useful when you already have data in another form and want an immutable copy of it.

from_list = tuple([1, 2, 3])
from_string = tuple("cat")
print(from_list)
print(from_string)

This prints (1, 2, 3) and then ('c', 'a', 't'). Notice that tuple() breaks the string into its individual characters, the same way it would break a list into its individual elements; it does not treat "cat" as one single item. An empty tuple, if you ever need one, is written () or tuple(), with no comma required since there is nothing to separate.
